name: Oxygen Access Project: oxygen care for hypoxaemic children in Gombe State, Nigeria (charityevals)
summary: Oxygen Access Project helps 23 state secondary hospitals in Gombe State, Nigeria, find children whose blood oxygen is low (below 90%) and treat them with oxygen, with the state hospitals board and the Nigerian NGO Taimaka. This model counts the children's deaths averted in its first financial year (14 February to 31 December 2025, about 660 hypoxaemic children recorded from April) against that year's spending, and comes to {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000. The biggest uncertainty is how many deaths better oxygen care averts here: before-after studies of oxygen systems found pneumonia deaths falling by about half, but the one randomised trial in Nigeria found no further fall once pulse oximetry was in place, and the charity has not yet measured who got oxygen or who died. So the effect is discounted for weak evidence and the model for missing data.

Share of the hypoxaemic children recorded who are newborns (under 28 days)
rows.explainer: The charity doesn't report ages or say whether newborn units report. In Graham's twelve Nigerian secondary hospitals, which counted newborn and children's wards alike, newborns were 51% of the hypoxaemic patients (1,363 of 2,667, Table 3), so half, from a quarter (if newborn units report less) to 60%.

rows.label: Death risk in hospital of a hypoxaemic child (28 days to 14 years) with the care these hospitals gave

source.title: Graham et al. (2019), Hypoxaemia in hospitalised children and neonates: a prospective cohort study in Nigerian secondary-level hospitals, EClinicalMedicine 16:51-63
source.page: Table 3, Total children (hypoxaemia 10.2%, case fatality 4.2%, crude odds ratio of death 9.2, 7.7-11.0)

rows.explainer: Worked from the cohort's crude figures for children: 10.2% hypoxaemic, 4.2% of all children died, and the hypoxaemic had 9.2 times the odds of death (the crude ratio, which splits a crude death rate; the adjusted 7.3 doesn't). Solving for the two groups gives about 19% of hypoxaemic children dying against 2.5% of the rest; by age band the same (infants 20%, one to four 18%, five to 14 18%). The range takes the odds ratio's interval, and runs higher for the cohort's partial oxygen care (some hospitals improved oxygen during it, so the risk without care is higher). The charity's own site cites about 2 in 10.

source.title: Graham et al. (2019), Hypoxaemia in hospitalised children and neonates: a prospective cohort study in Nigerian secondary-level hospitals, EClinicalMedicine 16:51-63
source.page: Table 3, Neonates <28 days (hypoxaemia 22.2%, case fatality 9.9%, crude odds ratio of death 6.2, 5.2-7.3)

rows.explainer: Worked the same way from the newborns' crude figures: 22.2% hypoxaemic, 9.9% died, crude odds of death 6.2 times higher, so about 26% of hypoxaemic newborns died against 5.4% of the rest; the range from the odds ratio's interval, and higher for the cohort's partial oxygen care.

rows.label: Admitted children and newborns screened for low blood oxygen, April to December 2025
rows.explainer: The programme has the facilities measure admitted children's blood oxygen and treat those below 90% with oxygen. The charity reports the hypoxaemic children found, not the children screened, so the screened are worked back from the share found hypoxaemic in Nigerian secondary hospitals. The deaths averted don't depend on this: the same shares turn the screened back into the 660 hypoxaemic children in hypoxaemic_share_screened.

rows.label: Cost per person reached
rows.explainer: Context: compare with the charity's own figure and with other models of the family.

rows.label: Illness episodes per child counted
rows.explainer: Each child counts once, for the one admission in which low oxygen was recorded: the death risks below are per admission, not per year.

rows.label: Share of the children screened who were hypoxaemic
rows.explainer: The recorded hypoxaemic children over the children screened: only they can be helped by oxygen.

rows.label: Risk of dying while hypoxaemic, per child screened, per admission
rows.explainer: The hypoxaemic share times their death risk, children's and newborns' weighted by the newborns' share. Per admission, not per year: each child counts for one admission (years_of_coverage).

rows.label: Fall in a hypoxaemic child's death risk with a working oxygen system

source.title: Lam et al. (2021), Oxygen systems strengthening as an intervention to prevent childhood deaths due to pneumonia in low-resource settings: systematic review, meta-analysis and cost-effectiveness, BMJ Global Health 6:e007468
source.quote: We calculated a pooled OR of 0.52 (95% CI 0.39 to 0.70) in favour of oxygen systems reducing childhood pneumonia mortality.

rows.explainer: Oxygen systems (pulse oximetry, concentrators, training, maintenance) cut childhood pneumonia deaths by 48% (30% to 61%) across four non-randomised studies in Papua New Guinea, Laos and Nigeria. That fall is over all pneumonia deaths; oxygen acts on the hypoxaemic children, whose deaths were about two thirds of the pneumonia deaths in Graham's Nigerian hospitals (28% hypoxaemic, crude odds of death 6.0 times higher, 7.2% dying: 0.665), so over their deaths alone it is about 0.48 / 0.665 = 0.72. The range runs from the pooled interval's low end over a higher share of deaths to its high end over a lower one. How far these before-after designs can be trusted is internal_validity_adj.

rows.label: Fall in a hypoxaemic newborn's death risk with a working oxygen system

source.title: Graham et al. (2019), Improving oxygen therapy for children and neonates in secondary hospitals in Nigeria: stepped-wedge cluster randomised trial and cost-effectiveness study, PLoS Medicine 16(11):e1002951
source.page: Table 3, Neonate rows (full oxygen system against preintervention, severity-adjusted aOR 0.90, 0.65-1.24)

rows.explainer: The only randomised evidence is the Nigerian stepped-wedge trial. Against care before the trial, the full oxygen system went with 10% lower odds of death for newborns once severity is adjusted for (0.90, 0.65 to 1.24; 0.97 unadjusted). Against the pulse-oximetry period alone it went with higher odds (1.45), which the authors put down to sicker newborns being admitted rather than harm from oxygen. The studies behind the children's figure didn't cover newborns. So a 10% fall, with the interval's range, which runs to harm.

rows.label: Fall in the death risk, children and newborns together (deaths-weighted)
rows.explainer: Each group's fall weighted by its share of the deaths, so deaths averted are children's and newborns' summed.
rows.formula: ((1 - neonatal_share) * child_cfr_hypoxaemic * child_mortality_reduction + neonatal_share * neonatal_cfr_hypoxaemic * neonatal_mortality_reduction) / ((1 - neonatal_share) * child_cfr_hypoxaemic + neonatal_share * neonatal_cfr_hypoxaemic)

rows.label: Indirect deaths per direct death averted
rows.explainer: 0: the death risks above are all in-hospital deaths of hypoxaemic children, whatever the cause, so there are no indirect deaths to add.

rows.label: Deaths averted per person reached (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Direct and indirect deaths over the years of protection. If the intervention protects several age groups with different risks, replace this formula with one row per group and sum them here; check the result against the all-cause trial result per person-year, scaled to today's mortality.

rows.label: Share of the deaths averted under age five
rows.explainer: Newborns and infants are the most often hypoxaemic and the most likely to die (in Graham's Nigerian hospitals hypoxaemia was 22% of newborns, 16% of infants, 9% of children aged one to four and 7% of those aged five to 14, with case fatality falling from 9.9% to 3.4%), and five-to-14-year-olds were 220 of the 1,300 hypoxaemic older children (Table 3). With newborns half of the hypoxaemic, about 93% of the deaths averted are under five, from 88% to 97%.

rows.label: Share of the deaths at five or older that are aged 5-14
rows.explainer: 1: the facilities' children's wards admit children up to 14, so no older deaths are counted.

rows.label: Share of the deaths at 15 or older that are aged 15-49
rows.explainer: Not used: no one aged 15 or older is counted (share_5_14_of_over5 is 1).

rows.label: Remaining life of a child saved, as a share of an average child's of the same age
rows.explainer: Children who survive a severe illness die in the months after discharge far more often than their age group (the site's shared figure; docs/normalization.md, survivors' remaining life), and hypoxia is one of the risk factors, so a death averted counts at this share of the value of a death at the child's age.

rows.label: Illness averted, as a share of the deaths' value
rows.explainer: Oxygen shortens the illness of the children who would have survived anyway and may spare some brain injury from low oxygen, but it doesn't avert the illness itself. The site's one figure for young children's respiratory infections, influenza's share of under-five burden that is years lived with illness (about 1%, GBD), is taken as the size of this.

rows.label: Stillbirths averted per child
rows.explainer: 0: the programme treats children already born.

rows.label: Later-life income gain per child, ln(consumption) a year
rows.explainer: 0: no study links oxygen during one illness to later earnings; the children's survival is counted as deaths averted.

rows.label: Years until the income gain begins
rows.explainer: Not used: no income gain is counted (ln_income_gain_per_year is 0); the site's shared figure stays so the row means the same in every model.

rows.label: Years the long-term income gain lasts
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for how long a long-term income gain lasts (GiveWell's working years, 40), read by every model that counts one (INV-13).

rows.label: Later-life income gain per person reached, present value
rows.explainer: Discounted at the shared rate, the wait included, so the result moves with it. Never type in a present value worked out elsewhere: rebuild it from its inputs.

rows.label: Resource sharing within households (multiplier on an earner's gain)
rows.explainer: The site's one figure (GiveWell's): an earner's income gain is shared with the household, so it counts this many times. Read by every model that values a long-term income gain (INV-13).

rows.label: Internal validity: how far the studies measured oxygen's own effect
rows.explainer: The pooled fall comes from before-after and non-randomised comparisons (risk of bias moderate, certainty low, as the review grades it), which also catch falling death rates from other causes. The one randomised comparison, the Nigerian stepped-wedge trial, found no further fall in children's deaths from the full oxygen system once pulse oximetry was in place (adjusted odds ratio 1.06, 0.77 to 1.46), though introducing pulse oximetry itself went with much lower odds of death for children with pneumonia (0.33, 0.12 to 0.92). Against care before the trial, the full system went with no fall in all children's deaths (severity-adjusted 1.03, 0.72 to 1.47; basic 1.05) but about half the deaths among children with pneumonia (0.50). Half of the pooled effect, from a quarter to most of it; after all the adjustments the model's fall in all child deaths is about a tenth, inside that trial's interval.

rows.label: External validity: whether a hypoxaemic child given oxygen here benefits as in the studies
rows.explainer: The setting is like the studies': Nigerian state secondary hospitals, with death risks at least as high in the north-east. One difference: the fall was measured on pneumonia, while the recorded children include hypoxaemic malaria, sepsis and febrile encephalopathy (in Graham's cohort pneumonia was 37% of the hypoxaemic children), where oxygen's benefit is less studied. 90%, from 60% to the same.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity), a multiplier
rows.explainer: The product of its two parts.

rows.label: Share of the improvement that others wouldn't have brought to these hospitals in 2025
rows.explainer: The studies' effect is already against their hospitals' care before the systems came (in the Nigerian trial's hospitals few used pulse oximeters, and half had oxygen for children), which is like Gombe's, so this asks only what differs: whether the state or another funder would have brought the same oximetry and oxygen care to these 23 facilities in 2025 anyway. No other oxygen programme is reported in these facilities, though the state could have improved some of them over the year; 85%, from 60% to 95%.

rows.label: Others' resources per hypoxaemic child treated (hospital staff time, oxygen, equipment), US$
rows.explainer: The state hospitals' clinical staff time, facilities and oxygen are theirs (the accounts don't count them) and would be spent anyway: co-funders' resources (Convention 2), at the extra cost of treating a hypoxaemic child with oxygen. A hypoxaemic patient in Graham's hospitals took oxygen for a median of 1.5 days (mean 2.8): about 3,500 litres for a newborn and 5,000 for an older child, plus nursing time and a share of a concentrator or cylinder; we judge this at $50, from $20 to $150.

rows.label: The charity's share of the resources behind the oxygen care
rows.explainer: Its cost per child screened against the hospitals' extra cost of treating, per child screened (only the hypoxaemic share, and of them the share treated, implementation_adj, use the hospitals' oxygen), so the shortfall isn't counted twice.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Oxygen coverage of the recorded hypoxaemic children, relative to the studies'
rows.explainer: The studies' effect already carries their own coverage: in the Nigerian trial's full-system period 81.6% of children below 90% got oxygen (694 of 851, Table 3), reached within 4 to 8 months. The charity reports the children recorded, not those treated, and in its first year it bought no equipment it kept (no fixed assets), relying on the hospitals' concentrators and supply, which break down; we judge about 70% treated, so 0.7 / 0.82, about 85% of the studies' coverage, from half to the same.

rows.label: Funging and leverage
rows.explainer: Its funders in 2025 and 2026 (Ambitious Impact, the Global Health Funding Circle, Effektiv Spenden) fund new charities; no government or large funder was paying for this work in these hospitals, so no money is displaced (1). Below 1 if the state would have funded it; above 1 if the work brings in state money later.

rows.label: Years a gift waits before it is spent
rows.explainer: Funds held at the year's end over a year's spending at 2025's rate.

rows.label: From spending to the children treated
rows.explainer: 0: the spending is the running programme in the same months as the children counted.

rows.label: Middle of the benefit
rows.explainer: 0: a death averted in one admission is a one-off effect.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the benefits come
rows.explainer: Every wait is discounted at the shared rate, like every future benefit (the income gain's own wait is counted from delivery, in ln_income_gain_per_person).

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin: the children recorded are the charity's own count, but who got oxygen and who died are not reported, and the effect comes from non-randomised studies of whole oxygen systems delivered by others, so the shared missing-data step applies. The charity plans a published external evaluation of impact and cost.

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.formula: evidence_adj * counterfactual_adj * attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount * missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Treatment costs averted
rows.explainer: 0: a treatment programme; it averts no treatment.

rows.label: Rebound
rows.explainer: 0: malaria prevention only.

rows.label: Investment of income gains
rows.explainer: 0: no income gain is counted.

rows.label: Other benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Training, reporting and repair habits built in 2025 that keep helping children after the year (+5%, 0 to +20%); against it, double counts or misrecorded readings in the weekly reports (about -2%, 0 to -10%). Net +3%, from -10% to +20%.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: GiveWell-style supplementary adjustments, each its own row, summed: they add to the modelled value as one share, as in GiveWell's sheets.

rows.label: Deaths averted
Value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's moral weights for the age band of each death averted, times your multiplier on the value of a life (the site's one value of a death, docs/normalization.md 2.7), times the saved children's shorter remaining life (survivor_remaining_life_ratio).

rows.label: Units of value from deaths averted
Units of value from stillbirths averted
rows.explainer: A stillbirth averted at the site's one value (@givewell_shared.uov_per_stillbirth, GiveWell's), times your multiplier on the value of a life.

rows.label: Units of value from later-life income
Units of value from illness averted
rows.explainer: A share of the deaths' and income's value, the base GiveWell's supplementary share has.

rows.label: Illness averted per child, in DALYs (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: 0: illness is counted as a share of the deaths' value (morbidity_value_ratio), never both.

rows.label: Illness averted, in DALYs
Illness averted, in units of value
rows.explainer: The bridge from DALYs into units of value: the unit's conversion cancels it, so illness counts as healthy years whatever "Healthy year vs doubled-income year" is set to.

rows.label: Total units of value
rows.explainer: Illness and the other supplementary shares add to the modelled value side by side, as one sum of shares does in GiveWell's sheets; illness counted in DALYs comes in through its bridge, inside the side-effect share like every other outcome.
